text: A jockey is a professional who rides horses in horse racing or steeplechase racing, and the term also applies to camel riders in camel racing. The word originated in England and was used to describe someone who rode horses in racing; it is a diminutive of "jock," a Northern English or Scots term for "John" or "boy," first recorded in 1529. In Shakespeare’s *Richard III*, the phrase "Jockey of Norfolk" appears. Originally, jockeys were all male, but female jockeys have since been allowed to compete, leading to many successful and well-known women in the sport. The term "jockey" was initially used in the 16th and 17th centuries for horse-dealers, postilions, itinerant minstrels, and vagabonds, often implying a trickster, and the verb "to jockey" meaning to outwit or deprive someone of something first appeared in that context. The current meaning of a race rider was first documented in 1670. Jockeys must be light, typically weighing between 100–120 lb (45–55 kg), and physically fit, with no official height limit, though they are usually short due to weight restrictions. Flat jockeys typically stand 4 ft 10 in (147 cm) to 5 ft 7 in (170 cm), while jump jockeys are often taller, with examples over 5 ft 10 in (178 cm); Lester Piggott, at 5 ft 8 in (173 cm), was nicknamed "Longfellow," and Jack Andrews, at 6 ft 4 in (193 cm), rides at 142 lb (64 kg); Bruce Hobbs, at 6 ft 1.5 in (186.7 cm), was the tallest jockey ever to win the Grand National. Jockeys are generally self-employed, nominated by trainers to ride their horses, and are paid a fee regardless of prize money and a percentage of the race winnings. In Australia, apprentice jockeys are employed under indenture to a master (trainer), and upon completing a four-year apprenticeship, they become senior jockeys and are considered freelance. Apprentices must successfully complete about 20 barrier trials before riding in races and are known as "bug boys" due to the asterisk symbol in race programs resembling a bug. All jockeys must be licensed and are not permitted to bet on races. Apprentices receive a weight allowance, allowing them to carry less weight than experienced jockeys in handicapped races, which incentivizes trainers to hire them. After their apprenticeship, senior jockeys may be paid a retainer by owners, giving the owner the right to require the jockey to ride their horses. Racing modeled on the English Jockey Club spread globally through colonial expansion. Jockeys wear the registered "colours" of their trainer or owner, a tradition rooted in medieval jousting and influenced by Italian city racing events, with traditional colours including purple, gold, or yellow/nude. The term "silks" refers to the white breeches and bib, stock, or cravat, and wearing silks is a rite of passage for new jockeys. Silks, which originated in the UK and were first mentioned in 1515, were formally established in the 1700s and are used to identify horses and owners; colours must be distinct and are registered by each Australian state’s Principal Racing Authority. Famous silks can be auctioned for high prices, reflecting their historical and cultural value. Jockeys must wear helmets, goggles, silks, vests, breeches, gloves, boots, saddles, girths, and stirrups during races, with safety vests worn beneath silks. The skivvy, a lightweight mesh or microfibre bodysuit, is worn under silks on race days and a heavier version during track work. Various annual awards are given to jockeys worldwide. The sport carries significant risks, including permanent, debilitating, and life-threatening injuries such as concussion, bone fractures, arthritis, trampling, and paralysis; jockey insurance premiums are among the highest in professional sports. Between 1993 and 1996, 6,545 injuries occurred, resulting in a rate of 606 per 1,000 jockey years. In Australia, race riding is considered the second most deadly job after offshore fishing, with five deaths and 861 serious injuries recorded from 2002 to 2006. Eating disorders, such as anorexia, are common due to the extreme pressure to maintain very low weights, often within a five-pound (2.3 kg) margin. The biography *Seabiscuit: An American Legend* documented these disorders, and cases like Kieren Fallon and Robert Winston highlight the physical toll of dehydration caused by weight restrictions. Sports Dietitians Australia warn that dehydration and energy depletion can impair concentration and coordination; research by the Irish Turf Club found that rapid weight loss leads to significant dehydration, though cognitive function is maintained, suggesting jockeys adapt to perform under dehydrated conditions. In January 2016, the International Concussion and Head Injury Research Foundation (ICHIRF) launched a study titled "Concussion in Sport," the first to examine concussion effects in athletes, including around 200 retired jockeys. In the U.S., women make up only 14% of working jockeys and ride only 10% of all race starts. In the 1850s, women-only events were held in Victoria, Australia, but women were not allowed to ride professionally or on men’s tracks. Wilhemena Smith rode as Bill Smith in north Queensland, using a male name and disguise, and was only officially recognized as a woman after her death in 1975. Elizabeth Williams Berry rode internationally as Jack Williams, disguising herself with cigars and a bowler hat. In Australia, female jockeys were restricted to "ladies only" events until the 1970s; the Victoria Racing Club allowed women to register for professional "ladies only" events in 1974, and New Zealand amended its rules in 1978. Pioneers like Pam O'Neill in Australia and Linda Jones in New Zealand pushed for equal competition, with O'Neill setting a world record on her first day. Bev Buckingham, Australia’s top female jockey, became the first in the Southern Hemisphere to win 1,000 races; she broke her neck in a 1998 fall at Elwick Racecourse but regained mobility. Clare Lindop won the Adelaide jockeys' premiership in 2004–05, becoming the first woman to win a metropolitan premiership in mainland Australia; Andrea Leek won the Grand National Hurdle in 2005. In 2009, women accounted for 17% of jockeys in Victoria but received only 10% of rides, especially in cities; about half of apprentice jockey intakes in some regions are women. In January 2015, all eight races at Mount Gambier were won by women jockeys. Michelle Payne became the first female jockey to win the Melbourne Cup on 3 November 2015. In Britain, women were banned from racing under Jockey Club rules, though records show women rode as men as early as 1804; Elizabeth Williams Berry rode in England as Jack Williams. In 1972, Meriel Patricia Tufnell won the first female race, the Goya Stakes; in 1976, Valerie Greaves became the first amateur woman to beat professionals under rules; in 1978, Karen Wiltshire became the first professional woman to win a British flat race. In 1996, Alex Greaves became the first woman to ride in the Epsom Dash. In the 21st century, women’s profiles rose in British flat racing: Hayley Turner became Champion Apprentice in 2005 and the first woman to ride 100 winners in a season in 2008; Kirsty Milczarek became the first woman to ride three winners at a single meeting in 2008, riding 71 winners that year. Amy Ryan and Josephine Gordon won apprentice championships in 2012 and 2016, respectively. In National Hunt racing, success has been limited, though amateur riders Nina Carberry and Katie Walsh (sister of Ruby Walsh) have won at the Cheltenham Festival. In 2010, both the winner and runner-up of a National Hunt Chase were ridden by women: Katie Walsh on Poker de Sivola and Nina Carberry on Becauseicouldntsee. On Boxing Day 2015, Lizzie Kelly won a Grade 1 race in Britain; she won another Grade 1 in 2017 at the Grand National Festival. In 2016, Rachael Blackmore became the first woman to win the Irish Conditional Jockeys title; in 2018, Lizzie Kelly became the first female professional to win at the Cheltenham Festival; in 2019, Bryony Frost became the first woman to ride a Grade 1 winner at Cheltenham; in 2021, Rachael Blackmore won the Grand National. The British Horseracing Authority encourages women, who make up three-quarters of graduates from the UK’s two main racing schools, to remain in the profession. In New Zealand, women constitute over 40% of jockeys; the first win by a woman was by Canadian jockey Joan Phipps in 1977. Linda Jones is believed to be the first New Zealand woman to apply for an apprentice licence, though she was denied, despite years of riding in lady rider events in New Zealand and abroad.

At the Cheltenham Festival, Bryony Frost became the first female jockey to ride a Grade 1 winner in 2019, riding Frodon in the Ryanair Chase. In 2021, Rachael Blackmore made history by becoming the first female jockey to win the Grand National, the most valuable jump race in Europe. The British Horseracing Authority (BHA) has been working to encourage the three-quarters of graduates from the two principal UK racing schools who are women to remain in the profession as jockeys. In New Zealand, women make up over 40% of jockeys in Thoroughbred racing. The first win by a woman in New Zealand was achieved by visiting Canadian jockey Joan Phipps at Te Awamutu in November 1977. Linda Jones is believed to be the first New Zealand woman to apply for an apprentice's licence, though she was rejected; she had previously ridden in lady riders events in New Zealand and overseas, including in Brazil, highlighting that New Zealand and Australia were outliers in not allowing women to compete with male jockeys in professional races. She eventually succeeded, and the New Zealand Racing Conference accepted female jockeys on 15 July 1978, with Joanne Hale (Giles) becoming the first New Zealand woman to ride in a totalisator race at Waimate that day. Sue Day (Christchurch), Joanne Lamond (Oamaru), and Vivienne Kaye (Awapuni) also rode in races on that day. Sue Day became the first New Zealand female jockey to win a totalisator race against males on 22 July 1978, winning with Jaws in the Waybrook Handicap at Timaru. Cherie Saxon (Hastings) was another female jockey active at the time. Linda Jones' first win was on Big Bickies at Te Rapa, followed by a win with Royal Petite, the first Open Handicap winner for a female jockey. Her other notable wins included Lovaro in the Queen Elizabeth Handicap and Holy Toledo in the Wellington Derby on 22 January 1979 (possibly the first female jockey worldwide to win a Derby). Jones was also the first female jockey to win a professional race against males at a registered meeting in Australia, winning aboard Pay The Purple in the Labour Day Cup at Doomben Racecourse, Brisbane on 7 May 1979. In 1982, Maree Lyndon became the first female jockey to win a Group I race in New Zealand, winning the New Zealand Cup on Sirtain. In 1986, Trudy Thornton became the first woman to ride in New Zealand's longest thoroughbred race, the Great Northern Steeplechase, and in 1995, Tina Egan became the first woman to win that race. In 1997, Catherine Hutchinson (née Tremayne) became the first female jockey to ride six winners in a day, achieving this at Ruakaka. Lisa Cropp won the New Zealand jockeys' premiership in 2005 and 2006. In recent years, the premiership has been won by Lisa Allpress (2012, 2016, 2019, and 2020), Samantha Collett (2018), and Danielle Johnson (2021). In April 2017 at Timaru, eight of the nine races were won by women jockeys: Alysha Collett, Kylie Williams, Tina Comignaghi, Amanda Morgan, and Samantha Wynne. On 10 October 2019 at Tauherenikau Racecourse, all eight races were won by women: Rosie Myers (4 races), Lisa Allpress (2), Charlotte O'Beirne (A), and Leah Mischewski. Eliza Carpenter (1851–1924) was an early African-American race horse owner in Ponca City, Oklahoma, where she trained horses and became one of the few African-American stable owners in the West; she sometimes rode her own horses as a jockey, winning some races, with recorded horses including "Irish Maid", "Blue Bird", "Jimmy Rain", "Sam Carpenter", and "Little Brown Jug", which she reportedly raced at Tijuana, Baja California. Anna Lee Aldred (1921–2006) received a license at age 18 in 1939 at Agua Caliente Racetrack in Tijuana, Mexico, when officials could not find a rule barring women jockeys, and she finished second by a nose in her first professional race. Hollywood stuntwoman Alice Van-Springsteen (1918–2008) also rode as a jockey and was one of the first women to receive a trainer's license for Thoroughbred horses. Wanta Davis (1918–2012) won over 1,000 races in the 1930s, 1940s, and 1950s, including a notable 1949 six-furlong match-race against Johnny Longden at Agua Caliente; she rode at some state-sanctioned pari-mutuel tracks without a license, with most events being dusty county fair or half-mile western circuit races, and although in demand as a training jockey, her license applications were repeatedly denied. Twelve years after Davis retired, the "modern era of female jockeys" began when Olympic equestrian and show jumping competitor Kathy Kusner, who had also ridden as a jockey, successfully sued the Maryland Racing Commission in 1967 under the Civil Rights Act, winning her case in 1968 and becoming one of the earliest women licensed in the United States, though an injury prevented her from racing. In late 1968, Penny Ann Early was the first woman to earn a mount as a licensed Thoroughbred jockey in the U.S., entering three races at Churchill Downs in November, but male jockeys boycotted those races, so she could not ride. On 7 February 1969, Diane Crump became the first licensed woman to ride in a parimutuel Thoroughbred race in the United States at Hialeah Park Race Track in Florida, requiring a police escort to reach the paddock. Two weeks later, on 22 February at Charles Town in West Virginia, Barbara Jo Rubin became the first woman to win a race, going on to win 11 of her first 22. Other women soon followed, and over time American women jockeys have proven their ability; Julie Krone has 3,704 victories, the most by an American woman, and as of June 2012, at least nineteen others have each ridden over 1,000 winners. Canada has generally followed the U.S. in opportunities for women jockeys, with only two female jockeys having over 1,000 wins, though in both actual and relative numbers and overall success rate, Canada has surpassed the U.S. in opportunities at the highest level, particularly in their respective Triple Crown series. Starting with Joan Phipps in the 1973 Breeders' Stakes, 10 different women have competed in 30 Canadian Triple Crown races, with a combined record of two wins, three places, and four shows. While no U.S. Triple Crown race has ever featured more than one female rider, that has occurred 10 times in Canada, with three women—Francine Villeneuve, Chantal Sutherland, and Emma-Jayne Wilson—racing in all three Canadian races, Sutherland doing it twice and Wilson three times. Since Diane Crump rode in the 1970 Kentucky Derby, six different women have competed in U.S. Triple Crown events, some multiple times: 10 times in the Derby, four times in the Preakness, and nine times in the Belmont, with a combined record of one win, one place, and one show. Julie Krone is the only woman to have won a U.S. Triple Crown race, on Colonial Affair in the 1993 Belmont. Rosie Napravnik became the first woman to ride in all three U.S. Triple Crown races with appearances in the 2011 Kentucky Derby, the 2012 Belmont Stakes, and the 2013 Preakness Stakes, and in 2013 she became the first woman to ride in all three U.S. Triple Crown races in the same year; she is also the only woman to have won the Kentucky Oaks, which she has won twice. To replace child jockeys whose use was deplored by human rights organizations, a camel race in Doha, Qatar, on 13 July 2005 featured robotic jockeys at the reins; seven camels were equipped with robots that operators controlled remotely, signaling them to pull reins and prod the camels with whips. In North America during the 1800s, most aspects of horse racing were primarily performed by enslaved African Americans; plantation owners brought enslaved workers and their horses to other plantations to organize and bet on races. Enslaved and free Black people were involved in horse racing, often in grooming, feeding, backing, exercising, and other auxiliary roles, eventually working up to becoming trainers and full-time racers. By the end of the 1800s, horse racing was almost exclusively run by African American jockeys, with Isaac Murphy, Willie Simms, and Jimmy Winkfield being the three most successful, Murphy winning the Kentucky Derby in 1884, 1887, and 1890. This dominance ended abruptly in 1896 after the Plessy v. Ferguson decision, which legalized segregation, leading to the end of African American jockeys' supremacy in the sport.
